text: I came in with a strong coding background but weaker theory, and I’d say this Data Structures course in the summer term hit more speed bumps than I expected. By the final week, the exams were straightforward but the pacing left me scrambling to connect a few dots between the practical code and the theory we skimmed in lectures.

text: Operating Systems with Prof. Rios was an advanced elective that I approached with mixed confidence—comfortable with proofs, but the systems side felt like stepping into a maze I wasn’t sure I’d navigate. Early on I was engaged, showing up with notes and a real curiosity about concurrency, but by mid-semester my attendance faded as the workload and the week-to-week pace didn’t sync with how I was juggling another hard class. The peer discussion sections saved me more than the official materials ever did; talking through race conditions and the locking diagrams with classmates made the lectures land, even when the slides felt patchy or uneven from week to week. I would have liked clearer guidance on how the grading would unfold—things felt transparent enough when the rubric finally dropped, but the months-long ambiguity during the term was frustrating. Tooling setup was a practical drag—getting the VM running and the environment configured took more time than it should have, and emails to support sometimes felt like shouting into a quiet room when deadlines loomed. There was a lot I learned, but I didn’t enjoy the overall experience as a cohesive ride.

text: Calculus II was a last-semester sprint I didn’t quite expect to enjoy as much as I needed to, since I was juggling it with a looming graduation timeline and a habit of leaning on recordings and notes more than live lectures. The exams felt fair in the sense that the questions aligned with what we actually practiced, but the practical rhythm was odd: the lectures often wandered into topics where I wasn’t sure how we’d apply them, while the assessments pulled from a different pace altogether. I’m comfortable with proofs, not systems work, so the parts about sequences and series integration clicked for me, yet the problem sets sometimes seemed to assume a comfort level I didn’t share, building on prerequisites in ways that didn’t always translate from the book to the board. Office hours saved the course more than once, with a few patients explanations that finally connected a stubborn convergence test to a concrete example I could annotate in my notes. Feedback felt sparse until after deadlines, which didn’t help when I needed to adjust my approach, and I’d only recommend it to someone who’s prepared to do extra legwork. Overall, I learned a lot, but I disliked the occasionally rough experience enough to hesitate before recommending it broadly.
